## Q1
For the grammar S → AB; B → +AB \| ε; A → CD; D → \*CD \| ε; C → [S] \| x, find FOLLOW(A) and FOLLOW(C).

## Q1 - Options
(A) FOLLOW(A) = {], $}; FOLLOW(C) = {+, ], $}
(B) FOLLOW(A) = {+, ], $}; FOLLOW(C) = {\*, +, ], $}
(C) FOLLOW(A) = {*, $, [}; FOLLOW(C) = {*, [, $}
(D) FOLLOW(A) = {\*, ], $}; FOLLOW(C) = {+, ], $}

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q96

In S → AB, FIRST(B) contributes + to FOLLOW(A), and because B can derive ε, FOLLOW(S) = {], $} also contributes. In A → CD, FIRST(D) contributes \* to FOLLOW(C); D can derive ε, so FOLLOW(A) also contributes +, ], and $. Therefore FOLLOW(A) = {+, ], $} and FOLLOW(C) = {\*, +, ], $}.

## Q2
For the grammar S → AB; B → +AB \| ε; A → CD; D → \*CD \| ε; C → [S] \| x, identify the correct statement.

## Q2 - Options
(A) The grammar is left recursive
(B) The grammar needs left factorization
(C) [[x\*x]+x] is a valid sentence of the grammar
(D) The grammar has an SLR(0) parser

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q97

The grammar generates expressions made from x and bracketed S expressions, with D adding repeated multiplication and B adding repeated addition. Thus [[x\*x]+x] derives through C → [S], S → AB, and the recursive B/D productions. It is neither left recursive nor left-factored, and “SLR(0)” is not a parser class.

## Q3
For the grammar S → AB; B → +AB \| ε; A → CD; D → \*CD \| ε; C → [S] \| x, how many non-blank LL(1) table entries occur in the B and D rows?

## Q3 - Options
(A) B = 3; D = 4
(B) B = 6; D = 5
(C) B = 2; D = 3
(D) B = 1; D = 2

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q98

For B → +AB, FIRST is {+}, so M[B,+] is one non-blank entry. Because B → ε, put that production under every symbol in FOLLOW(B) = {], $}, yielding two more entries and B = 3. Likewise D → *CD gives M[D,*], while D → ε is entered for FOLLOW(D) = {+, ], $}; that is one plus three, so D = 4.

## Q4
For the grammar S → AB; B → +AB \| ε; A → CD; D → \*CD \| ε; C → [S] \| x, find FIRST(S) and FIRST(D).

## Q4 - Options
(A) FIRST(S) = {+, [, x}; FIRST(D) = {+, \*}
(B) FIRST(S) = {[, ], x}; FIRST(D) = {+, ε}
(C) FIRST(S) = {[, x}; FIRST(D) = {\*, ε}
(D) FIRST(S) = {[, x, ε}; FIRST(D) = {\*, ε}

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q99

S begins with A, A begins with C, and C begins only with [ or x, so FIRST(S) = {[, x}. D directly derives *CD or ε, hence FIRST(D) = {*, ε}.

## Q5
For the augmented grammar S′ → S; S → AB; B → +AB \| ε; A → CD; D → \*CD \| ε; C → [S] \| x, how many productions are in the I₁ state of the canonical LR(0) set?

## Q5 - Options
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 4
(D) 6

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q100

I₀ contains S′ → ·S together with the closure productions for S, A, and C. Taking GOTO(I₀, S) produces I₁ = {S′ → S·}; the dot is at the end, so no closure expansion is added. Thus I₁ has exactly one item/production.

## Q6
A phase of a compiler which produces the symbol table is

## Q6 - Options
(A) Syntax analysis
(B) Semantic analysis
(C) Target code generation
(D) Code optimization

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q4

Symbol table entries for identifiers and declarations are created as the parser recognizes declaration constructs while building the parse tree, so syntax analysis is the phase that produces the symbol table.

- **A. Syntax analysis** — correct. The parser creates symbol table entries while recognizing declarations in the grammar.
- **B. Semantic analysis** — this phase uses and updates existing symbol table entries with type and scope information, it does not originate the table.
- **C. Target code generation** — this phase consumes finalized symbol table information to generate machine code, long after the table already exists.
- **D. Code optimization** — this phase transforms intermediate code for efficiency and does not create symbol table entries.

## Q7
Arrange the following tasks of a lexical analyzer in the correct sequence.

A. Token Generation.<br>
B. Removal of comments/White sphere.<br>
C. Buffering and reading source characters.<br>
D. Return token stream to parser.

## Q7 - Options
(A) A, B, C, D
(B) B, A, C, D
(C) C, B, A, D
(D) B, A, D, C

## Q7 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q18

A lexical analyzer first buffers and reads the raw source characters, strips out comments and white space that carry no lexical meaning, groups the remaining characters into tokens, and then passes the resulting token stream on to the parser.

C-B-A-D — Buffering and reading source characters, Removal of comments/white space, Token Generation, Return token stream to parser — is the correct sequence.

## Q8
Match List-I (Compiler input) with List-II (Compiler phase).

| LIST-I (Input) | LIST-II (Compiler Phase) |
|---|---|
| A. Syntax Tree | I. Code Generator |
| B. Character Stream | II. Syntax Analyzer |
| C. Intermediate Representation | III. Semantic Analyzer |
| D. Token Stream | IV. Lexical Analyzer |

## Q8 - Options
(A) A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
(B) A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
(C) A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
(D) A-I, B-IV, C-II, D-III

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q32

Each pairing follows from what each compiler phase consumes as its input.

A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

- **A. Syntax Tree — III. Semantic Analyzer.** The parser produces the syntax tree, and the semantic analyzer consumes it to check types and scope.
- **B. Character Stream — IV. Lexical Analyzer.** The lexical analyzer is the first phase, reading the raw source code character by character.
- **C. Intermediate Representation — I. Code Generator.** The code generator takes the intermediate representation and translates it into target code.
- **D. Token Stream — II. Syntax Analyzer.** The lexical analyzer hands its stream of tokens to the syntax analyzer, which parses them against the grammar.

## Q9
Arrange LL(0), LR(0), SLR, LALR(1), and LR(1) parsers from least to greatest grammar-handling power.

## Q9 - Options
(A) LL(0) → LR(0) → SLR → LR(1) → LALR(1)
(B) SLR → LR(0) → LL(0) → LR(1) → LALR(1)
(C) LL(0) → LR(0) → SLR → LALR(1) → LR(1)
(D) LR(0) → LL(0) → SLR → LR(1) → LALR(1)

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q51

LL(0) has no lookahead and is most restricted. LR(0) adds bottom-up item sets, SLR uses FOLLOW sets to reduce conflicts, LALR(1) merges compatible LR(1) states, and canonical LR(1) retains the most lookahead information. Hence C gives the increasing order.

## Q10
Which high-level program corresponds to the displayed three-address code?

![q91-tac-code-options.png](https://media.thewholetest.com/ugc-net/2025-june-1/paper-2/q91-tac-code-options.png)

```text
100: t1 = y+2
101: initial = x/t1
102: limit = 10
103: if i>j goto 105
104: goto 111
105: if num > b goto 107
106: goto 111
107: num = limit-1
108: b = y+2
109: i = i - num
110: goto 103
111: j = i - num
112: k = j+b
```

Three-address code and its four high-level-code alternatives.

## Q10 - Options
(A) Source code option 1
(B) Source code option 2
(C) Source code option 3
(D) `init = x/(y+2); limit = 10; while (i > j && num > b) { num = limit-1; b = y+2; i = i-num; } j = i-num; k = j+b;`

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q91

The two conditional jumps send execution to the loop body only when both `i > j` and `num > b` hold. The loop body recomputes `num`, `b`, and `i`, then jumps back to the first condition; on either failed condition it computes `j` and `k`. That control flow is the `while` form in option D.

## Q12
Consider the grammar:

S → A<br>
A → $B$ \| id<br>
B → B, A \| A

If I₀ = CLOSURE({[S → .A]}), how many items are in GOTO(I₀, $)?

## Q12 - Options
(A) 3
(B) 4
(C) 5
(D) 6

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q1

GOTO(I₀, $) begins with A → $.B. Its closure adds B → .B, A, B → .A, A → .$B$, and A → .id, giving five items in total. Therefore option C is correct.

## Q13
Consider the Grammar:<br>
T → Qx<br>
Q → RS<br>
R → y ∣ ϵ<br>
S → z ∣ ϵ<br>
Here x, y, z are terminals and T, Q, R, S are non- terminals.<br>
What will be the follow set of the non-terminal R?

## Q13 - Options
(A) {x,y}
(B) {y,z}
(C) {z,x}
(D) {ϵ}

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q18

In Q → RS, whatever can begin S follows R, contributing z. Because S can also derive ε, anything following Q follows R as well, and T → Qx supplies x. Hence FOLLOW(R) = {z, x}, which is option C.

## Q14
Which of the following tasks could be attained using syntax trees in compiler design ?<br>
A. Type Checking<br>
B. Code Generation<br>
C. Code Optimization<br>
D. Error Handling

## Q14 - Options
(A) (A), (B), (C) Only
(B) (B), (C), (D) Only
(C) (A), (C), (D) Only
(D) (A), (B), (D) Only

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q51

A syntax tree is the structured representation the compiler walks for type checking (A), code generation (B) and code optimisation (C). It can reveal that an error exists, but recovering from errors is the job of the error-handling machinery rather than the tree itself. Only (A), (B) and (C) — option A.
